blocks.text: Ezekiel's prophetic call begins with a command to stand. When he does, the Spirit enters him and sets him upright, enabling him to hear the divine voice. Throughout this calling account, the Spirit and hand imagery appear as characteristic features of Ezekiel's prophetic experience, marking the supernatural empowerment that defines his commission.

God sends Ezekiel to Israel, a nation marked by continuous rebellion against the Lord from ancient times through the present. This mission places Ezekiel within the prophetic tradition of Israel's monarchy, temple, and exile periods. Biblical prophets differed from royal seers by speaking directly with the Lord's authority, and they functioned as covenant messengers and watchmen—roles that define Ezekiel's calling to a resistant people.

Whether Israel hears or refuses to listen, the people will know that a prophet has lived among them. Yet resistance is certain: they are a rebellious house, and Ezekiel will face their defiance. He is warned not to fear their words or their hostile looks, even though he dwells among them as one surrounded by thorns and scorpions. His duty remains constant—to speak God's words to them regardless of their response. This pattern of prophetic witness amid refusal, combined with watchman responsibility even toward a resistant audience, frames Ezekiel's entire ministry.

Ezekiel is instructed to consume what is placed before him. A hand extends to him bearing a scroll inscribed on both sides with lamentations, mourning, and woe. The act of eating the written word becomes a core element of his commissioning. Eating the scroll, receiving the prophetic message, accepting the watchman role, and speaking under divine constraint all weave together as interconnected dimensions of Ezekiel's calling.
